unit.can_do_en: make a shopping list and follow a simple recipe.

brief.situation_en: Aino reads the recipe to Maria.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: First peel the potatoes and carrots.

judge.reason: 'Eka' is the spoken form of 'ensin' (first); the rest is identical.
Okei/selvä are both acknowledgements, and sit/sitten both mean 'then'.
The spoken pieniks paloiks is the same as the written pieniksi paloiksi (into small pieces).

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.text_puhe: Joo, hyvä. Laita ne kattilaan ja lisää vettä.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä, hyvä. Laita ne kattilaan ja lisää vettä.
lines.gloss_en: Yes, good. Put them in the pot and add water.

judge.reason: Joo and kyllä both mean 'yes'; the instructions are the same.

puhe.text: Joo, hyvä. Laita ne kattilaan ja lisää vettä.

kirja.text: Kyllä, hyvä. Laita ne kattilaan ja lisää vettä.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: A litre. Boil for twenty minutes.

judge.reason: Kakskyt minuuttii is the spoken form of kaksikymmentä minuuttia (twenty minutes); litra is unchanged.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: And the salmon goes in last?

judge.reason: Vikana is the spoken form of viimeisenä (last); the meaning is unchanged.

forms.why_en: Speech often uses the short word eka. Books write ensin.
Kuoria, to peel. To tell one person to do it, drop the ending: kuori.
Adds -t for more than one: peruna becomes perunat.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -t for more than one: porkkana becomes porkkanat.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
Speech shortens sitten to sit. Books write sitten.
Leikata, to cut. To tell one person to do it: leikkaa. The k doubles in this form.
Ne means they, for things. Speech also uses it for people.
Adds -ksi for 'into': pieni becomes pieniksi, 'into small (pieces)'. Speech drops the last i.
Pala, piece. Many pieces plus -ksi for 'into': paloiksi. Speech drops the i: paloiks.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is how you tell someone to put: laita. It comes from laittaa, with one t.
Adds -an for 'into': kattila becomes kattilaan.
Lisätä, to add. To tell one person to do it: lisää.
The partitive singular is used for some water: vesi becomes vettä, the si turning to tt.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Keittää, to boil. To tell one person to do it, drop the ending: keitä. The tt becomes t.
Speech shortens kaksikymmentä to kakskyt. Books write kaksikymmentä.
After a number the noun takes the partitive: kymmenen minuuttia. Speech turns -ia into -ii.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Tulla, to come, in the form for he, she or it: tulee.
Adds -nä to say how or in what role: viimeinen becomes viimeisenä. Speech uses vika: vikana.
